abstract: Global energy demand has historically been provided for by fossil fuels. As energy demand continues to rise in response to increasing population and industrialization, the use in fossil fuels will also rise. This rise is anticipated to have negative impacts on our global environment in the form of environmental risk factors. Therefore, a switch in energy dependency from fossil fuels to clean renewable energy is necessary to mitigate these risk factors. To make this transition, we envision a zero-emission pathway by harnessing energy from the sun in the form of solar fuels. By harnessing solar energy via a photovoltaic, electrons will be provided to reduce CO2 to CO. The well-known Fischer-Tropsch process will then use CO as the C1 feedstock to produce the solar fuels. ☐ For the initial transformation, the Rosenthal Research Lab developed a bismuth carbon monoxide evolving catalyst (Bi-CMEC), prepared by an acid aqueous electrodeposition bath. Its ability to selectively (>90 %) and efficiently (83 %) electrocatalytically transform CO2 to CO with the incorporation of imidazolium-based ionic liquids (ILs) was demonstrated. Bi relates to the historic Ag and Au cathodes in the ability to selectively evolve CO, but is not impeded by the cost of material when used on an industrial scale. ☐ To further encourage industrial integration of Bi-CMEC and to enhance these impressive metrics, I helped with the development of a 3D-printed flow electrolysis assembly for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CO. 3D printing allows for rapid and cost effective prototyping with high precision and accuracy. The flow cell is a sealed system which does not require constant operation or system re-optimization. Importantly, the flow cell recycles electrolyte and encourages faster mass transport from the constant flow of fresh electrolyte across the electrode surface. Here, we have modified existing drop casting techniques to screen a slew of inexpensive and commercially available Bi3+ salt precursors. We also took advantage of inexpensive carbon supports to further the likelihood of transitioning this chemistry into industry. Our progress with Bi-CMEC preparation and industrial cell design truly highlights the feasibility of integrating a Bi-based CO2 electrolyzer into industry. ☐ Mechanistic insights for Bi-CMEC to facilitate this transformation were studied with Tafel analysis and MD calculations performed in a collaborative effort with the University of Minnesota and co-workers of the Rosenthal Research Lab. Specifically, Tafel analysis suggested that the rate determining step (RDS) for Bi-CMEC is the first electron transfer (ET) to yield the surface bound CO2•–. MD simulations agreed with the first ET being rate limiting and highlighted the role of surface bound IL and IL in the solution bulk. Upon developing an organic plating procedure, in situ studies were performed which offered additional insight for the catalytic behavior of Bi-CMEC. The organic electrodeposition procedure was general and allowed for materials other than Bi (Sn, Pb, and Sb) to be studied. The ability of these p-block metals to reduce CO2 to CO was explored and ultimately revealed unique electrochemical behaviors. Despite Sb showing poor activity for CO2 reduction, Bi, Sn, and Pb demonstrated high CO selectivity (~80 %) with current densities for CO generation ranging from 5–8 mA/cm2. While Bi and Sn both showed impressive electrochemical behaviors, Pb demonstrated film passivation and CO2 activation occurred at a larger overpotential. These initial studies inspired curiosity as to why these materials, when prepared in a similar manner, demonstrated unique catalysis. ☐ To understand why Pb becomes passivated, I performed extensive studies on the RDS, electrochemical events, and surface adsorbate interactions for the Bi, Sn, and Pb cathodes. Tafel studies performed on the Pb cathode suggested that an adsorbate forms on the surface to block charge transfer events. Surface studies were subsequently performed to identify the evolution of adsorbates for the Bi, Sn, and Pb cathodes. While Bi and Sn were nearly identical, Pb demonstrated an additional impurity adsorption component. This component was later identified as an imidazolium-carboxylate adduct. This adduct was found to exist both on the surface and in solution for Pb, but was not identified in either medium for Bi or Sn. ☐ Imidazolium-carboxylate is highlighted in the literature to be an essential intermediate for the stabilization of CO2•– to lower the activation energy of this redox reaction. Because this theory disagrees with our previous experimental results, I performed thorough studies on the adduct itself. Here, direct information on its electrochemical behavior and participation in catalysis were observed. It was revealed that the adduct formation is irreversible, such that it creates a thermodynamic sink upon formation during electrolysis. When the adduct exists in solution, it was found to interfere with the diffusion of reactants and products migrating to and from the electrode surface to negatively impact the current density. For Bi and Sn specifically, the adduct interferes with the cathode/IL interaction at the surface without formally adsorbing. The IL monolayer becomes loosely adsorbed and no longer suppresses hydrogen production to selectively favor CO evolution. ☐ IL serves multiple purposes during catalysis including stabilizing the electrode bias, providing protons for the 2H+/2e– redox reaction, and functioning as electrolyte. Therefore, I was interested in observing how neat IL systems would compare to the organic system with dilute IL. Additionally, ILs are a greener solvent compared to organics and would further help with industrial integration. For these studies, the essential cathode/IL interface remained, but the inherent physical properties of the IL electrolyte became more prevalent, i.e. viscosity, symmetry, intermolecular interactions. The higher solution viscosity was shown to drastically reduce mass transport. Poor diffusion was remedied with temperature enhancement. Here, it was found that Sn-CMEC was more durable than Bi-CMEC for extreme reaction conditions. Thus, temperature studies were continued with Sn-CMEC. Temperature studies were performed with 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium hexafluorophosphate ([BMIM]PF6) and 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium trifluoromethanesulfonate ([BMIM]OTf). Interestingly, the durability of these ILs were found to be highly dependent on the anion. [BMIM]OTf demonstrated high selectivity and current density up to 100 ⁰C, whereas [BMIM]PF6 showed no positive correlation to any temperature range. These differences were due to the durability (decomposition temperature) of each IL. ☐ To enhance mass transport for [BMIM]PF6 without sacrificing the durability of the IL during catalysis, admixtures of acetonitrile were added. This revealed fascinating chemistry, such that there is now a switch in catalytic dependency. Remarkably, the electronic behavior became less resistive to facilitate charge transfer, mass transport, and CO selectivity. Importantly, the IL did not show evidence for significant decomposition. These IL studies highlight electrochemical behavior of IL during electrolysis.

abstract: Macromolecular materials play a pivotal role in (opto)electronic and energy storage applications. Achieving high performance materials necessitates a profound comprehension of the intricate interplay between macromolecular structures and (electronic) function. One illustrative case is the design of polymers tailored for electron transport as semiconductors or conductors, which often features an extended π-conjugated system, triggering a cascade of necessary design rules and limitations. The research into these structure-function interdependencies is highly dynamic and our understanding of them is constantly evolving, allowing us to continuously increase material performance and also to devise new applications. At the same time, new developments and emerging applications are expanding the spectrum of criteria used to evaluate material performance. The parameter space that must be considered now encompasses interactions with biological systems throughout and beyond the device's lifespan, i.e., markers of biocompatibility and transience. Once again, understanding the structure–function relationships is crucial. This understanding becomes paramount, for instance, in achieving the delicate balance between ion permeability and electron transport for interfacing with biological tissues, modulating the Young's modulus of a polymeric semiconductor for wearables, or to include structurally weak points in the molecular system to facilitate controlled degradation or recycling. This special issue on “Macromolecular Structures for Electronics, Optoelectronics, and Energy Storage” features a collection of 13 research papers and 3 review articles. These contributions delve into various facets of the relationship between macromolecular structure and function, collectively underscoring the essential nature of a comprehensive understanding of this interdependency in the pursuit for high performance materials. Examples are provided across the diverse fields of polymer synthesis, processing (including 3D techniques), controlled degradation, and application-driven investigations spanning photovoltaics, energy storage, wearable electronics and logic circuits. The synthesis of conjugated polymers is commonly achieved by transition metal catalyzed polycondensations using aryl monomers with organometallic groups and aryl halides in a stochiometric ratio. Direct arylation polymerization emerges as an atom-economical and more sustainable alternative to conventional synthetic methods. Wang et al. (Article 2300245) report a direct arylation polymerization using brominated thienoisoindigo, thereby extending the accessible monomer pool. Takimoto et al. demonstrate a nonstoichiometric direct arylation polycondensation using a dual catalyst, a biphasic solvent system and under mild conditions, which promote an intramolecular catalyst transfer (Article 2300225) In conjugated polyelectrolytes, the π-conjugated backbone carries ionic groups, adding ionic charge transport to the more thoroughly investigated electric charge transport. Schmidt et al. use controlled Kumada catalyst transfer polymerization in conjunction with a polymer-analog substitution to obtain regioregular anionic polythiophenes. The defined lengths of the systems allow the systematic investigation of their optical properties in aqueous solution (Article 2300396). The most extensive category of polymers in the field is characterized by their π-conjugated backbones. In contrast, the backbone of non-conjugated pendant electroactive polymers (NCPEPs) contains saturated carbons, and tethered electroactive pendant groups bring the needed optical and electronic properties. This structural design offers the intriguing possibility to significantly enlarge the available synthetic toolbox. In their review, Schmitt et al. summarize structure-property relationships of NCPEPs and how their (opto)electronic properties can be controlled by tuning the molecular structure (Article 2300219). In addition to de novo synthesis, controlling the packing arrangement through processing provides another functional handle for tuning physical properties. In their article, Li et al. introduce a versatile solvent additive strategy aimed at modulating aggregation, enabling precise control over crystal size and orientation in donor-acceptor polymers (Article 2300288). Meanwhile, Daoulas et al. present a qualitative theory describing the relationship between lamella orientation and the elastic and electronic properties of semiconducting polymers (Article 2300437). After decades of fundamental research into the synthesis and processing of conjugated polymers, a wealth of knowledge has been amassed regarding their structure-property relationships. This robust foundation has catapulted the field into an application-driven one, wherein the design and development of new conjugated polymers are precisely tailored to optimize performance for specific applications. Photovoltaics is one of the most extensively studied applications for π-conjugated macromolecular structures. Singlet-fission-capable polymers emerge as a particularly promising class of materials with the potential to significantly improve the power conversion efficiency of organic solar cells. This enhancement is achieved by the conversion of a higher energy singlet exciton into two lower energy triplet excitons. The review article from Wang et al. provides an overview of the recent advancements and the challenges within this burgeoning field (Article 2300241). Energy storage devices are indispensable to modern life. The rich redox chemistry inherent in π-conjugated macromolecular structures offers an efficient route to store charges, a theme explored in two articles within this issue. Zuo et al. introduce a conjugated microporous polytriphenylamine, templated by carbon nanotubes, that shows high redox activity and electrical conductivity (Article 2300238). Meanwhile, Chang et al.’s fundamental investigation yields valuable insights into the degradation mechanism of conducting polymer-based pseudocapacitors, offering potential avenues to enhance the cycling stability of such devices (Article 2300237). Using π-conjugated macromolecular structures for wearable sensors for healthcare monitoring has emerged as a vibrant area of research in recent years. This application requires a balance between electrical properties and mechanical extensibility, which are traditionally conflicting attributes. The review article from Guo et al. provides a comprehensive overview of the field (Article 2300246). Specifically, doping strategies to synergistically improve both electrical and mechanical properties are delineated. In a complementary exploration, Sung et al. studied the mobility-compressibility properties of contact-transferred isoindigo-bithiophene with carbosilane side chains (Article 2300058). This work illuminates a relatively under-explored topic, as most existing studies predominately focus on mobility-extensibility relationships. Blending conjugated polymers in an elastomer matrix is an efficient way to achieve stretchable electroactive films. In their article, Qin et al. elucidate the process of mechanical fracture during stretching by investigating the blend of a lowly-soluble benzothiadiazole-based copolymer in a highly soluble elastomer (Article 2300240). Multi-functionality is a coveted trait in the realm of next-generation devices, a theme explored in two research articles in this special issue. Wessling et al. demonstrate that phenothiazine-based donor-acceptor polymers can be used to both harvest solar energy via bulk heterojunction photovoltaics and simultaneously storing charges in lithium-organic batteries (Article 2200699). While emphasizing the promising capabilities of this material, the authors also acknowledge the inherent challenges in balancing performance for both applications using a single material, as some degree of compromise is required. In a parallel investigation, Xuyao et al. illustrate that the diketopyrrolepyrrole-based copolymers exhibit both highly balanced ambipolar charge transport while proving suitable for integration into high-voltage logic circuits (Article 2300271). This work showcases the potential for multi-functionality in advanced organic electronic devices. A number of emerging areas are also represented by articles in this special issue. While the field of additive manufacturing has been growing at a rapid pace, the 3D printing of conjugated polymers remains challenging due to their sensitivity to processing conditions. Lopez-Larrea et al. present a new approach to 3D print conductive poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrenesulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) hydrogels by using visible light (Article 2300229). This method not only addresses some of the existing hurdles, but also unlocks geometric freedom and design flexibility for conjugated polymers. These new form factors, in combination with enhancement in electrical and mechanical performances, is anticipated to usher in a new realm of application possibilities for conjugated polymers. Extending our focus beyond material performance and device applications, our society grapples with a pressing dilemma concerning polymer waste. π-Conjugated macromolecular structures are not exempt from the issue, especially given their expanding application space. Bartlett et al. describe an environmentally conscious synthesis of azomethine-containing pyrrolo[3,2-b]pyrrole copolymers that can be degraded back to their monomeric units, offering a sustainable solution for end-of-life management (Article 2300220). We are pleased to present this special issue on “Macromolecular Structures for Electronics, Optoelectronics, and Energy Storage.” The contributions underscore the significance of the relationship between macromolecular structure and function, highlighting the critical role this link plays in the development of high-performance materials across diverse fields, ranging from energy storage to solar cells and wearable electronics. We thank all the contributors to this issue. Our hope is that this collection not only catalyzes the generation of new ideas and concepts, but also promotes conversations among researchers across different disciplines. Finally, we extend our gratitude to the editorial team of Macromolecular Rapid Communications, with special thanks to Deputy Editor, Dr. David Huesmann, for their collaborative efforts in bringing this issue to fruition. The authors declare no conflict of interest. Yue Jessica Wang received her PhD from the University of California, Los Angeles in 2014. Subsequently, she carried out postdoctoral research at Stanford University before joining the University of California, Merced in 2017. She is currently an Assistant Professor of Materials Science and Engineering, and has affiliated appointments in the Chemistry and Biochemistry and the Bioengineering departments. Her research focuses on developing bioinspired and bio-designed polymers and structures with unconventional physical properties. Franziska S.-C. Lissel is a Professor heading the Institute of Applied Polymer Physics at the Hamburg University of Technology and the Functional Electronic Materials group within the Leibniz Institute of Polymer Research (IPF) Dresden. Her group develops electronically active polymers, organic and hybrid materials and seeks to understand structure-property relationships in molecular and organic electronics. Previously, she was associated with Prof. Z. Bao (Stanford), and obtained her Ph.D. with Prof. H. Berke (Zürich 2014).

abstract: MOON EXPLORATION{ PART 1 }Prepared by:ENG. MAJD ALSADILAMIA SHAHEENAffiliation: MENA ORG ANALOG MISSIONPresented at:International Astronautical Congress (IAC) 2025Sydney, AustraliaJuly 2025AbstractThe Moon, Earth’s closest celestial neighbor, continues to inspire scientific exploration. As a natural satellite, it offers a unique opportunity to study the formation and evolution of the solar system. This research paper highlights the importance of lunar exploration, reviewing key missions, technologies, and the scientific and strategic benefits of returning to the Moon.The study emphasizes how lunar geology contributes to understanding planetary origins, and how the Moon serves as a testing ground for space technologies supporting future missions to Mars and beyond. It also explores in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), such as the presence of water ice in polar regions, and current efforts to develop sustainable lunar habitats.Despite major advances, challenges remain, including radiation, low gravity, and logistical constraints. Through continuous innovation and international cooperation, the Moon remains a vital gateway for deep space exploration and the future of human presence beyond Earth.IntroductionThe Moon, being the closest celestial body to Earth, has long fascinated scientists and explorers. With the rapid advancement of space technology, this fascination has evolved into direct scientific exploration—from early uncrewed missions to the historic Apollo 11 landing in 1969.Lunar exploration extends beyond understanding the Moon’s geology; it provides a pathway to study the origins of the solar system and Earth itself. More importantly, it offers a platform to support long-term human space missions to other planets, primarily Mars.In recent years, global interest in the Moon has resurged, positioning it as a strategic stepping-stone for deeper space exploration. Space agencies around the world are actively investigating lunar resources, environmental conditions, and infrastructure development for sustainable human settlement.The 21st century has shifted the Moon’s role from a symbolic target to a practical destination. Missions now focus on establishing long-term presence, utilizing local resources, and testing life-support technologies necessary for future interplanetary travel. Lunar exploration is no longer just a vision; it is an ongoing scientific and strategic endeavor.By combining robotic and human missions, the Moon becomes more than a stopover—it becomes a frontier for innovation, collaboration, and a new era of space living. The coming decades hold vast potential for turning the Moon into a foundation for humanity’s expansion into the solar system.2. Orbital and Robotic Missions on the MoonLunar exploration has seen remarkable progress thanks to both orbital and robotic surface missions. These missions play a crucial role in collecting data and analyzing the Moon’s environment without risking human life.2.1 Orbital MissionsThese spacecraft orbit the Moon and gather detailed images, terrain data, and compositional analysis of the lunar surface. Notable missions include:• Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) – Launched by NASA in 2009 to provide high-resolution maps and surface characteristics.• Chandrayaan-1 – India’s 2008 mission that contributed to the discovery of water molecules on the lunar surface.• SELENE (Kaguya) – A Japanese mission that delivered topographical data and insights into the Moon’s interior structure.2.2 Robotic Surface MissionsThese missions land directly on the Moon and use landers or rovers for in-depth exploration.• Luna Missions – Soviet missions (1959–1976) that marked the first successful landings and sample returns.• Surveyor Program – American landers in the 1960s that tested soft-landing techniques for future crewed missions.• Chang’e Program – China’s modern lunar program, with landers like Chang’e 3 and Chang’e 4, and rovers such as Yutu (Jade Rabbit), which explored the Moon’s far side.2.3 Mission Significance• Created detailed topographic maps of the Moon.• Identified potential water ice deposits.• Tested precision landing and remote operations.• Prepared for future human missions by analyzing surface hazards and resources.3. Human Missions and Lunar SettlementsAs space technology evolves, agencies are shifting focus from short-term landings to long-term human presence on the Moon. Lunar exploration is now central to developing permanent settlements and preparing for missions to Mars.3.1 Artemis ProgramLed by NASA, in collaboration with ESA, JAXA, and other partners, Artemis aims to return astronauts to the Moon—particularly the south pole, where water ice is likely present.The mission phases include:• Initial uncrewed test flights of systems.• A crewed landing featuring the first woman and first person of color on the Moon.• Utilization of SLS rocket and Orion capsule for transportation.3.2 Lunar GatewayA small modular space station planned for lunar orbit, serving as a staging point for Moon landings and deep-space missions. Its roles include:• Providing logistical and life-support infrastructure.• Serving as a science lab and docking hub.• Reducing reliance on direct Earth launches.3.3 Lunar Habitats and ConstructionCurrent research focuses on building sustainable lunar bases, using local materials such as regolith (lunar soil) and:• 3D printing technologies for habitat construction.• Closed-loop life support systems powered by solar energy.• Studying long-term effects of lunar conditions on human health.These initiatives aim to make the Moon a permanent human outpost, enabling long-duration missions and reducing dependency on Earth-based supplies.4. Life Sciences and Lunar Resource UtilizationUnderstanding the lunar environment and adapting to it is essential for the success of long-duration human missions on the Moon and beyond. This involves addressing the effects of low gravity and space radiation, while developing sustainable life support systems and agricultural solutions.4.1 Effects of Low Gravity and Radiation on Human Health:The Moon’s gravity is about one-sixth that of Earth, which directly affects muscle mass, bone density, circulation, and spatial orientation. Moreover, the Moon lacks a protective atmosphere and magnetic field, exposing astronauts to galactic cosmic radiation (GCR) and solar particle events (SPE).Ongoing biomedical studies examine:• Muscle atrophy and bone loss.• Changes in cardiovascular and nervous systems.• Impacts on sleep, balance, and sensory functions.Preventive measures being researched include:• Radiation shielding materials using lunar regolith.• Building shelters in lava tubes or subsurface craters.• Medical supplements and antioxidants to reduce cellular damage.3D Illustration of a Lunar Colony4.2 Lunar Agriculture ResearchFood independence is critical for long-term lunar missions. Current agricultural research includes:• Growing crops in controlled inflatable greenhouses.• Hydroponic and aeroponic farming in sealed systems.• Studying plant growth in low gravity conditions.Goals:• Develop self-sustaining food systems.• Minimize resupply from Earth.• Generate oxygen and clean air through photosynthesis.4.3 In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU)ISRU aims to use local lunar materials to support missions and reduce cost and complexity. Key resources include:• Water ice in permanently shadowed craters, usable for drinking water, oxygen, and hydrogen fuel.• Lunar regolith, rich in silicon and titanium, for construction and industrial use.• Helium-3, a rare isotope that holds potential for nuclear fusion energy in the future.Establishing ISRU systems will allow the Moon to serve as a strategic logistics hub for Mars missions and other deep space exploration.5. Preparatory Activities for Solar System ExplorationThe Moon serves as an ideal testing ground for advanced technologies required for deep space missions, particularly those targeting Mars. Its proximity to Earth and exposure to harsh space conditions make it a realistic environment for experimenting with:• Closed-loop life support systems, which recycle air and water and maintain a stable living environment.• Advanced propulsion technologies for precise landing and ascent in low-gravity conditions.• Biomedical equipment tailored for isolated and resource-limited environments.• Autonomous communication and robotic systems, which will be essential in crewed and uncrewed Mars missions.These activities are essential for improving human readiness and system reliability, positioning the Moon as a training platform before venturing deeper into the solar system.6. International and Private Sector CollaborationLunar exploration has transformed into a collaborative global effort involving both space agencies and private companies. This shared approach accelerates innovation, reduces costs, and broadens participation.6.1 Collaboration Among Space Agencies• NASA, in partnership with ESA (Europe), JAXA (Japan), and CSA (Canada), is working on programs like the Lunar Gateway.• India (ISRO) and China (CNSA) continue to lead advanced robotic missions with plans for future crewed lunar operations.• Agencies exchange scientific data, infrastructure, and mission standards, ensuring interoperability and synergy.6.2 Role of the Private Sector• Companies like Astrobotic and Intuitive Machines collaborate with NASA through the Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program to deliver scientific and commercial cargo to the Moon.• These companies are developing:o Precision landing systemso Mobile roboticso Payload delivery infrastructureThis international-public-private model is reshaping lunar exploration—from a government-dominated domain to an open and cooperative ecosystem, fostering faster progress and sustainable growth in space science and commerce.7. abstract: The fair-trade system has made commodities from coffee to cocoa and gold more sustainable, but can it do the same for plastic? Affirmative, according to recent research showing that an ethical product standard for plastic 3D printing filament could lift garbage pickers out of poverty while reducing the global deluge of plastic trash (J Sustain Dev 2014; doi:10.5539/jsd.v7n5p1). “The price of 3D printers is plummeting and the market for printers and filament is exploding”, explains study coauthor Joshua Pearce, a materials scientist at Michigan Technological University (Houghton, MI). A 3D printer feeds a spool of plastic thread, or “filament”, into a heated extruder and lays down thin layers of plastic to build anything from kitchen spatulas to limb prostheses. Conventional filament made of virgin plastic can cost US$50 per kilogram. But 2 years ago, Pearce and his team developed a low-cost desktop “recyclebot” that turns plastic waste such as discarded milk jugs into filament using only US$0.10 of electricity per kilogram of filament. The recycled filament could potentially sell for one-tenth of the price of conventional filament. 3D printers using fair-trade plastic could reduce poverty and pollution. During a conversation with William Hoyle, CEO of techfortrade, a UK charity (London), Pearce says, “We realized that the price gap between conventional and recycled filament provided an opportunity whereby waste pickers in the developing world could transform a cheap material into something valuable”. The idea is that consumers would rather pay a premium for 3D printer filament that is not made from raw material collected by poor people, including children, without proper compensation. And because of the price gap, fair-trade filament would still outcompete its conventional counterpart based on cost. So Pearce and his group proposed ethical product standards for filament, including a minimum price to ensure fair wages, labor and environmental safeguards, and processes to invest in education and health care. Using Pearce's ethical filament standards, techfortrade launched the Ethical Filament Foundation and has licensed Protoprint, a company in Pune, India, to sell fair-trade 3D printer filament. Protoprint partners with waste picker cooperatives, sets up filament labs at dump sites, and trains workers to clean, shred, and extrude filament. The IUCN Red List, first published 50 years ago, is considered the most comprehensive global inventory of species' conservation status. On the basis of measures of population size and habitat loss, species are grouped into risk categories from Least Conservation Concern to Critically Endangered. The Red List, however, was not developed to explicitly consider climate-change impacts. Although numerous approaches exist to identify climate-vulnerable species, none have yet been tested for their ability to provide advanced warning for conservation actions. To determine whether the IUCN Red List was up to the task, a team led by Resit Akçakaya (Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY) forecasted population dynamics for range-restricted amphibians and reptiles in North America under three climate-change scenarios. Since inadequate data exist to conduct detailed models for all individual species, the team combined projected spatial distributions with generic life-history models for a typical snake, small salamander, large salamander, turtle, tortoise, and lizard. The framework yielded 9720 hypothetical populations that were then used to model the incremental impacts of climate change. The paper (Glob Change Biol 2014; doi:10.1111/gcb.12721) found the Red List could provide at least 20 years of “warning time” (defined as years recorded within a threatened category before extinction) but suggests that conservation actions should begin as soon as a species is listed as Vulnerable. “The average length of warning time at the Critically Endangered level is only 20 years”, says Akçakaya, adding that, “We cannot delay conservation action until a species is at the highest threat level”. Conservation actions typically follow a two-pronged approach; targeted efforts are focused on Critically Endangered animals – most often imperiled as a result of overhunting or habitat destruction – but far more dollars are spent on habitat protection efforts aimed at numerous species of lower-level concern, according to Russ Mittermeier, chair of the IUCN Primates Specialist Group. Cost, however, is a key hurdle. A recent paper (Science 2012; 10.1126/science.1229803) estimated that a US$1 billion annual investment –only 12% of which was funded at the time of the study – would be necessary to reduce the extinction risk of globally threatened bird species in the coming decade. Stuart Butchart, head of science at BirdLife International (Cambridge, UK), says Akçakaya's approach could be further developed to list species as threatened, based on their estimated extinction probability over 100 years. Scientists have puzzled over how toxic flame retardant chemicals (FRs) make their way into streams and coastal waters, where they are taken up by aquatic species from mussels to whales. Now a first-of-its-kind study traces one key pathway: FR-contaminated dust particles in households “hitch a ride” on clothing and other laundry items and are transported with residential wastewater through sewage treatment plants and into receiving waters, where many of the compounds survive chemically intact (Environ Sci Technol 2014; doi:10.1021/es502227h). The annual global use of FRs has been estimated at upward of 1.5 million metric tons, and continues to rise as increasing global populations demand more and newer products. Added to countless consumer goods and building materials, from fabrics and furniture to electronics and insulation, these long-lived compounds are now ubiquitous on lands and in waters worldwide. Indoor environments are also contaminated with FRs, many of which are linked to cancer, hormone disruption, neurotoxic-ity, reproductive impacts, and other harmful effects. A research team led by Erika Schreder, Science Director at the Washington Toxics Coalition (Seattle), investigated the role households could play in channeling FRs to freshwater and marine environments. They looked into 20 homes from two Washington State towns, testing dust and rinse water from washing machines for 22 FRs. They also screened for the same chemicals in samples of sewage water going into and coming out of two wastewater treatment plants that discharge into the lower Columbia River. The researchers detected 21 FRs in household dust and 18 in laundry water, with most of the compounds showing up in 95% of the households. They identified PBDEs (poly-brominated diphenyl ethers) – now banned or being phased out – as well as newer formulations of chlorinated organophosphate retardants, which were present at the highest concentrations of all the FRs found in treatment plant discharges. Based on levels measured in this water, the analysis estimates a yearly discharge of 174 kg (384 lbs) of FRs to the river from just one treatment facility. “This study fills a gap in information on how FRs are getting to our waters, and shows what happens when we use them in products in our homes”, Schreder says. “If manufacturers follow the lead of companies that have replaced these compounds with safer materials, and policy makers require companies to take toxic FRs out of products, we can put an end to this major pollution pathway.” Researchers using a metric that accounts for the spatial pattern of roads in an area (“roadless volume” or RV) report that road building impacts bird communities in southern Amazonia not only by promoting deforestation but also through fragmenting habitat and causing more subtle environmental effects such as microclimate changes (P R Soc B 2014; doi:10.1098/rspb.2014.1742). “Road density and distance from roads have been used in the past to examine how roads impact biodiversity”, explains Sadia Ahmed (Microsoft Research, Cambridge, UK), “but we wanted a more solid metric that would allow us to combine satellite imagery and ground data to estimate the effect of road networks on biodiversity. Notably, although more calibration of the RV metric is needed, our results suggest that, by combining information on RV change and forest cover change, it might be possible to identify regions of future biodiversity loss.” The chestnut-tailed antbird (Myrmeciza hemimelaena) is strongly affected by the presence of roads. Major road-building programs are underway in many developing countries. In Brazil, for example, road networks grew by almost 17 000 km every year between 2004 and 2007. Road expansion in developing countries brings important socioeconomic benefits to human populations but negatively affects the natural environment. Previous studies have investigated these impacts by measuring the effect of road density on biodiversity; however, Ahmed maintains this is insufficient: “The spatial pattern of road development isn't captured by this metric. A new road in a frontier region has much more impact than the same length of road in an area that already has roads.” In their study, the researchers measured bird species richness and community composition at 18 sites in the State of Pará, in northern Brazil, and used satellite-based data to calculate the RV of the sites. They found a positive correlation between RV and forest bird species richness and composition at the study sites. However, there was no significant correlation between RV and forest cover, which suggests that road networks affect biodiversity independently of forest loss. “Although based on a fairly small sample size, this is an important study”, comments tropical ecosystem expert William Laurance (James Cook University, Cairns, Australia). “The road avoidance effect in forest birds can be surprisingly strong and this study tells us that if we do have to build roads in sensitive habitats, we should minimize them and try to locate them on the margins of critical habitats, rather than cutting through the heart of that habitat.” A new study (Global Ecol Biogeogr 2014; doi:10.1111/geb.12206) reveals that future fall seasons in the Northern Hemisphere may last longer, bringing welcome news for tourists seeking beautiful vistas of colorful autumn leaves. Coauthors David Medvigy and Su-Jong Jeong (Princeton University, Princeton, NJ) have previously modeled patterns of seasonal changes, but only recently developed a single model that can predict autumn leaf-off times across the entire US. “Fall leaf coloration marks the end of the growing season in temperate climates, so understanding its current and future cycles sheds light on what is to come for agriculture, water supplies, and animal behavior”, says Medvigy. Compiling enough data on the patterns of different deciduous tree species has limited earlier efforts to model leaf-off times successfully. “A major challenge to modelers has been the lack of observations of individual trees across large spatial scales”, explains Medvigy. Using field observations from sites across the US, the authors filled in some of the data gaps and produced a much more robust model – and, in fact, identified a large geographic component in predicting leaf-off time. Interspecific variation in timing of leaf coloration complicates development of phenological models. “[We found that] the timing of leaf coloring is more sensitive to temperature in warmer areas than in colder regions”, explains Medvigy. “For the same increase in fall temperature values, tree species in Massachusetts would respond to a greater degree than species in Alaska. With northern locations experiencing smaller changes and southern areas experiencing larger ones, this could lead to an extended coloration season under climate change.” Longer autumn seasons could have big impacts on agriculture, influencing both the types and productivity of crops planted, as well as associated pest species. Ecologically, fall seasons that are prolonged and have later starting times may affect animal feeding cycles and regional water availability. One of these researchers' future aims is to better understand the implications for carbon sequestration in a changing climate. A longer, later autumn could translate into an extended growing season and therefore greater potential carbon sequestration by forests. “In general, we hope that this work will permit better forecasts for climate and for basic forest dynamics”, concludes Medvigy. Building on an idea that originated with Charles Darwin, a new hypothesis suggests that invasive species are more likely to originate from regions with relatively higher phylogenetic diversity, whereas less diverse areas are at greater risk of invasion. The authors of the study (Glob Ecol Biogeogr 2014; doi:10.1111/geb.12221) argue that a combination of factors – such as large, historically stable habitats and intense interspecies competition – may drive the evolution of diverse, efficient, and highly adapted competitors. Their Evolutionary Imbalance Hypothesis predicts that these species, when introduced into similar habitats in less diverse regions, tend to outcompete native species and turn invasive. “Some species may become invasive simply because they're better adapted”, says study coauthor Dov Sax of Brown University (Providence, RI). Despite its proposal long ago in Darwin's On The Origin of Species, this concept – that invasiveness is an outcome of natural selection – has largely been absent from modern approaches to invasion biology, which focus instead on ecological factors influencing invasions, such as habitat disturbance and enemy release, according to the study. To test their hypothesis, the authors examined species exchanges, including patterns of plant invasions between biotic regions. They used phylogenetic diversity as a proxy to represent the genetic potential, historical stability, and competitive intensity in different global regions. Sax and his colleague found that, as predicted, species that invade regions with lower phylogenetic diversity are more likely to have originated from areas with higher phylo-genetic diversity. “Species from other regions invade New Zealand, but we don't see many species from New Zealand invading other regions”, Sax points out. They also studied the exchanges of fish and mollusk species that have occurred between previously isolated areas recently connected by canals. After the Suez Canal effectively joined the Red Sea with the less diverse Mediterranean Sea, the flow of species was overwhelmingly from the former into the latter body of water. The authors believe that conservation managers analyzing the risk of invasions should consider the phylogenetic diversity of introduced species' native regions. There may be other ecological implications: if invasive species succeed in part because they use resources more efficiently, their presence might result in higher overall biomass production in invaded habitats. “Though the news is definitely bad for native species, it's possible that these invasive species might actually increase ecosystem function”, Sax suggests. On September 23, over 150 companies, governments, and organizations endorsed the UN's New York Declaration on Forests, pledging to halve tropical deforestation by 2020 and eliminate it by 2030. Cargill, Inc, one of the 40 industry signatories, announced that it would apply the zero deforestation promise to all the commodities it produces, including cattle, palm oil, soybeans, sugar, and cocoa. The commitment from the US$137 billion agriculture giant exemplifies the unprecedented aim and scope of the declaration. “Commercial agriculture is responsible for 70% of tropical deforestation”, says Elizabeth Baer, a corporate engagement manager with the World Resources Institute (WRI, Washing-ton, DC). Worldwide, deforestation contributes up to 20% of annual greenhouse-gas emissions. “Legal policies are insufficient to protect forests from deforestation, so the reach of Cargill's commitment has the potential to shift the way agriculture is done”, she continues. Cargill hasn't provided details on turning its pledge into practice, but the company could draw on recent innovations, according to Baer, who has spoken with Cargill about WRI's tools. In terms of defining zero deforestation, “cutting primary forests is off the table, while cutting scrub growing on abandoned farms would be okay”, she explains. But it's not clear what can be done with marginal land that falls between these two extremes. “Cargill has committed to determining just where on the land its palm oil comes from”, Baer says. Tracing the supply is complicated because the company buys the oil from so many producers. The key is combining sophisticated accounting systems with real-time maps such as WRI's Global Forest Watch. Using satellite data and user-generated reports, Global Forest Watch creates maps that show where deforestation is occurring and whether it is on protected land. Once the company is able to trace its supply chain, Global Forest Watch could verify that the commodities were produced without deforestation. WRI estimates that achieving zero deforestation and restoring degraded forests by 2030 worldwide could reduce atmospheric emissions by around 4–6 gigatons of CO2 equivalent per year, a greater emissions reduction than removing every car, bus, and plane from the US, China, and India combined. But can the declaration succeed in time? Globally, only about 15% of forest cover remains intact and 20% has been degraded. However, over the past year, 60% of the palm oil trade has gone deforestation-free. “We don't know if cutting deforestation by half by 2020 will be soon enough, but it's exciting and a good start”, Baer declares. Giant clams glitter under water and, according to new findings, this sparkle is created by reflective clam cells that direct light for the benefit of symbiotic algae. Researchers have long known that photosyn-thetic algae of the genus Symbiodinium live inside Tridacnid “giant” clams, which grow with their mouth-like gapes pointed toward the light. Decades ago, scientists identified iridescent cells known as iridocytes in the mantle tissue of these clams, but they could only speculate that the cells supported the symbiotic algae. To shed light on the physical function of irido-cytes, Alison Sweeney of the University of Pennsylvania (Phila-delphia, PA) and her colleagues built fiber-optic probes capable of measuring the light inside clam tissue. The findings are the first to describe the role of iridocytes in clam–algae symbiosis (J R Soc Interface 2014; doi:10.1098/rsif.2014.0678).
